entries.title: Awadhi / Lucknowi Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Awadhi cuisine: the Nawabs of Oudh, the dum pukht slow-cooking technique, and the legend behind Lucknow's melt-in-the-mouth galouti kebab.
entries.text: awadhi / lucknowi cuisine awadhi/lucknowi cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of awadhi cuisine: the nawabs of oudh, the dum pukht slow-cooking technique, and the legend behind lucknow's melt-in-the-mouth galouti kebab. awadhi/lucknowi cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana nawabi north awadhi / lucknowi cuisine the refined court cooking of the nawabs of oudh. sealed-pot slow cooking, gentle spicing, and kebabs made to dissolve on the tongue. a cuisine built for a court, not a marketplace awadhi cuisine takes its name from awadh (oudh), the region around lucknow ruled by the nawabs of oudh from the early 18th century until the british annexed it in 1856. the nawabs began as mughal provincial governors. as central mughal authority weakened, they became independent rulers in practice while keeping mughal court culture, including its cooking, as their model. what developed in lucknow's royal kitchens over the following century was less about heat or heavy spicing than about refinement. technique and aroma mattered more than raw chili, and the cooking was aimed at an audience of one, the nawab, rather than a marketplace of customers. dum pukht and a famine-relief legend dum pukht, literally "breath-cooking," is the defining awadhi technique. meat and rice are sealed into a heavy pot, often with a rim of dough, and cooked slowly over a low, steady fire, so the dish finishes in its own trapped steam and aroma rather than direct heat. lucknow legend ties its popularization to a famine around 1784, when nawab asaf-ud-daula commissioned the bara imambara as a relief-work project. food for the laborers was reportedly cooked overnight in huge sealed deghs (cauldrons) so it would be ready whenever a shift ended. whether or not that story is literally true, it captures what the technique was built for. this is cooking that holds its quality over long, unpredictable stretches of time. "dum pukht" literally means "breath-cooking." the food finishes in its own trapped steam inside a sealed pot, not over open heat. galouti kebab: built for a nawab who had lost his teeth lucknow's best-known dish has a similarly specific legend behind it. the galouti kebab ("melt-in-the-mouth" kebab) is said to have been created for an aging nawab, often identified as asaf-ud-daula or wajid ali shah, who loved kebabs but had lost his teeth. the cooks pounded the meat exceptionally fine and worked in a complex spice blend, popularly (if probably apocryphally) said to run to over a hundred spices. the result was a kebab soft enough to need no chewing at all. lucknow's tunday kebabi, named for its founder's tunda (disabled arm), still trades on a version of that closely guarded recipe today. biryani, the awadhi way awadhi biryani is usually cooked pukki style. the rice and meat are parboiled and cooked separately, then layered and finished together under dum. that gives a drier, more distinctly layered result than hyderabad's kacchi biryani, where raw marinated meat and raw rice go into the pot together from the start. the two techniques, developed in two different nawabi courts, remain the clearest fault line in indian biryani-making. awadhi cooking also travelled well beyond lucknow. when the british exiled the last nawab, wajid ali shah, to calcutta in 1856, he brought his court cooks with him. bengal's own kolkata-style biryani, distinguished by the addition of potato, is usually traced to that exiled awadhi kitchen adapting to leaner circumstances. quick facts region awadh, central-northern uttar pradesh (capital: lucknow) staple grain wheat and rice defining technique dum (sealed slow-cooking) and finely pounded meat key historical moment semi-independent rule by the nawabs of oudh, 18th century to 1856 signature dish galouti kebab galouti kebab: finely pounded, richly spiced meat, designed to need no chewing at all. nihari: a slow-simmered meat stew, traditionally served for breakfast. signature dishes galouti kebab : finely pounded, heavily spiced kebab, said to have been created for a toothless nawab. lucknowi (pukki) dum biryani : rice and meat parboiled separately, layered, then finished under dum. nihari : a slow-simmered meat stew, traditionally a breakfast dish. sheermal : a mildly sweet, saffron-tinted flatbread. zarda : sweet saffron rice, often served to close a meal.

entries.title: Bengali Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Bengali cuisine: river fish, mustard oil, and the invention of rosogolla in 19th-century Kolkata.
entries.text: bengali cuisine bengali cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of bengali cuisine: river fish, mustard oil, and the invention of rosogolla in 19th-century kolkata. bengali cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana east india bengali cuisine a rice and fish delta cuisine with a sweet tooth precise enough to be its own art form. a cuisine built by a river delta bengal sits on the ganges-brahmaputra delta, one of the most fertile and water-rich regions on earth, and its food reflects that directly. rice is the staple, and freshwater and river fish (hilsa/ilish above all) are the main protein. mustard grows across bengal's fields and supplies both the seeds for pungent mustard-paste sauces and the oil that bengali cooking is built on. where punjab cooks in ghee, bengal cooks in mustard oil, and that difference defines the cuisine as much as any spice does. a meal with a structure a traditional bengali meal isn't served all at once. it moves through courses in a set order. it starts with something bitter (shukto, a mixed-vegetable dish) to wake up the palate, then rice and dal, then a vegetable dish, then fish or meat curry, then chutney, and finally something sweet. that's closer to a french tasting menu than to the single-plate thali found across most of the rest of india. the meal is paced as a sequence rather than assembled on one plate. where most of india treats sweets as dessert, bengal treats them as a technical discipline in their own right. the invention of rosogolla bengali sweets stand apart because of one technique. cooks curdle milk into chhena (fresh cheese) and shape it into desserts, which is unusual in indian sweet-making. most of the rest of the country relies on reduced milk (khoya) or dough instead. the most famous result, rosogolla (spongy chhena balls in sugar syrup), is credited to kolkata confectioner nobin chandra das around 1868. some food historians trace the cheese-curdling method back further, to portuguese traders and missionaries who brought cheese-making to bengal centuries earlier. that makes rosogolla a 19th-century bengali invention built on a much older imported technique. sandesh, a firmer chhena sweet often flavored with jaggery, developed alongside it as the other pillar of bengali confectionery. calcutta and colonial-era influence as the capital of british india until 1911, calcutta had more direct contact with european cooking than most indian cities of its time. anglo-indian dishes, western-style cutlets and chops, and a citywide restaurant and confectionery culture all grew out of this period. they layered onto the older rice-fish-mustard base of home cooking. quick facts region west bengal (and historically undivided bengal) staple grain rice defining technique mustard oil & mustard-paste cooking; chhena (fresh cheese) sweets key historical moment rosogolla's invention in 1860s kolkata signature protein freshwater & river fish, especially hilsa (ilish) rosogolla (rasgulla): spongy chhena balls in sugar syrup, invented in 1860s kolkata. shorshe ilish: hilsa fish cooked in a pungent mustard-seed paste. signature dishes machher jhol : a light, everyday fish curry. shorshe ilish : hilsa fish in mustard sauce, arguably bengal's most iconic dish. kosha mangsho : a slow-cooked, dark, richly spiced mutton curry. rosogolla (rasgulla) : spongy chhena balls in sugar syrup. sandesh : a firmer chhena sweet, often flavored with jaggery. mishti doi : sweetened, slow-fermented yogurt.

entries.title: Bihari Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Bihari cuisine: sattu as everyday protein, litti chokha baked over embers, the Magadha and Mithila kitchens, and the sweets of Gaya, Silao and Maner.
entries.text: bihari cuisine bihari cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of bihari cuisine: sattu as everyday protein, litti chokha baked over embers, the magadha and mithila kitchens, and the sweets of gaya, silao and maner. bihari cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana east india bihari cuisine a gangetic plain cuisine built on roasted gram, mustard oil and live embers, feeding more people on less than almost any kitchen in india. sattu, the flour that does the work of meat if one ingredient explains bihar, it is sattu: chana roasted whole and then stone-ground into a nutty, high-protein flour. it needs no cooking, keeps for weeks without refrigeration, and costs very little. that combination made it the everyday protein of a densely populated, largely agricultural state, and it turns up in almost every meal. whisked into cold water with black salt, lemon and green chilli it becomes sattu sharbat, drunk by the glass through a bihari summer. spiked with garlic, ajwain and mustard oil it stuffs parathas and litti. the rest of the pantry is the gangetic plain's: wheat and rice, mustard oil pressed sharp, panch phoran for the tempering, and freshwater fish from the ganga, gandak and kosi. bihari cooking is not subtle in the way awadhi cooking next door is subtle. it is direct, sour with lemon and amchur, hot with raw mustard oil and green chilli, and it leans on smoke and char rather than long-simmered gravies. litti chokha, and cooking without a stove litti is a ball of wheat dough packed with seasoned sattu and baked hard in the ashes of a cow-dung or coal fire, then cracked open and drowned in ghee. chokha, its partner, is roasted brinjal, tomato and potato mashed with raw onion, mustard oil and lemon. the pairing is the state's best-known dish, and its logic is the logic of field food: it needs no pan, no stove and no gravy, it travels, and it keeps. that ember-baked technique gave bihar a reputation as poor food, which it has spent the last two decades shedding. litti chokha now turns up in patna restaurants and delhi food halls, and the dish has become a marker of bihari identity well beyond the state. litti needs no pan, no stove and no gravy. it is field food that outlived the field, and it now carries a state's name. magadha, mithila, and two different kitchens bihar is not one food region. the south and centre — old magadha, with pataliputra at its heart, the seat of the mauryan empire and the ground on which both buddhism and jainism took shape — leans vegetarian, wheat-heavy and austere. the north, across the ganga, is mithila: the maithil brahmin and kayastha kitchens of darbhanga and madhubani, where fish is everyday food rather than an exception, and rice displaces wheat. a maithil wedding feast and a magadhi one look very different. the northwest has its own claim. champaran, on the nepal border, gave india ahuna mutton — meat, mustard oil, garlic and whole spices sealed inside an earthen handi with dough and cooked slowly over its own steam, the pot broken open at the table. it is the one bihari dish that is unapologetically rich. sweets with addresses bihari sweets are unusually place-specific: each belongs to a named town and is judged against it. silao, near nalanda, makes khaja, a layered fried pastry soaked in syrup that carries a geographical indication tag. gaya makes tilkut, sesame and jaggery pounded together by hand in winter workshops for makar sankranti. maner makes laddus. thekua, ridged wheat biscuits fried in ghee, are made for chhath, the four-day festival of the sun god that is the most important date in the bihari calendar and whose offerings are cooked under strict rules of purity. the state's newest recognition is agricultural rather than culinary. mithila makhana — foxnut, popped from the seeds of a water lily grown in north bihar's ponds — received a gi tag in 2022, and the crop has become one of the region's few genuine export successes. quick facts region bihar and jharkhand, the middle gangetic plain staple grain wheat in the south and centre, rice in mithila defining technique ember-baking; sattu fillings; panch phoran tempering in raw mustard oil key ingredient sattu, roasted gram flour signature protein freshwater fish, mutton, gram and pulses champaran ahuna mutton: sealed in an earthen handi with dough and cooked in its own steam. tilkut being pounded by hand in gaya, made through the winter for makar sankranti. signature dishes litti chokha : sattu-stuffed wheat balls baked in embers, dipped in ghee and crushed over smoky mashed vegetables. sattu ka paratha : flatbread stuffed with roasted gram flour, garlic, ajwain and mustard oil. sattu sharbat : roasted gram flour whisked into cold water with black salt, lemon and green chilli. champaran ahuna mutton : mutton slow-cooked in a dough-sealed earthen handi. chana ghugni : black or white gram simmered dry and finished with onion, lemon and chilli. dal pitha : steamed rice-flour dumplings stuffed with spiced chana dal. kadhi bari : gram-flour dumplings in a sour, turmeric-yellow buttermilk gravy. thekua : ridged wheat-and-jaggery biscuits fried in ghee, made for chhath. khaja : layered fried pastry in syrup, tied to the town of silao. cook a bihari dish tonight

entries.title: Goan Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Goan cuisine: 450 years of Portuguese rule, the origin of vindaloo, and the Hindu-Catholic culinary split.
entries.text: goan cuisine goan cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of goan cuisine: 450 years of portuguese rule, the origin of vindaloo, and the hindu-catholic culinary split. goan cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana coastal india goan cuisine 450 years of portuguese rule, folded into a konkani coastal tradition and preserved in the name of a single dish. the longest colonial presence in india goa was a portuguese colony from 1510 until 1961, roughly 450 years. that makes it by far the longest continuous european colonial presence anywhere in india (british rule, by comparison, lasted under 200 years). the length mattered. it gave portuguese ingredients and techniques time to genuinely integrate into local cooking rather than sit alongside it. the result is a cuisine that is authentically both konkani coastal and portuguese-iberian at once, rather than one simply borrowing from the other. vindaloo's name is a history lesson the clearest evidence is sitting in plain sight in the name of goa's best-known dish. vindaloo derives from the portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos , meat marinated in wine ( vinho ) and garlic ( alhos ). that was a preservation technique portuguese sailors used for meat on long sea voyages. in goa, wine vinegar was often substituted or supplemented with local palm vinegar, garlic remained central, and chili (a portuguese-introduced new world import) was added. a shipboard preservation method had become one of india's most recognizable curries. the dish's name is, essentially, a 500-year-old linguistic fossil. vindaloo's name literally means "meat, wine, and garlic" in portuguese. the recipe is a shipboard preservation trick that became a national dish. two goan cuisines, split by religion goa's food culture, like rajasthan's, really contains two distinct traditions, here split along religious lines. goan catholic cuisine, from the community most directly shaped by portuguese conversion and rule, centers on pork, beef, and vinegar-based dishes like vindaloo and sorpotel, alongside portuguese-derived desserts like bebinca, a rich layered coconut-and-egg cake. goan hindu cuisine, particularly that of the saraswat brahmins, stayed closer to the broader konkani coastal tradition, built on fish, coconut, and kokum, with far less portuguese influence and no pork or beef. both are unambiguously goan. they simply come from different communities within the same 450-year colonial history. cashews, chilies, and the wider ripple effect goa's port role also made it one of the entry points through which new world crops first reached the indian subcontinent, among them chilies, potatoes, tomatoes, and cashews, carried in on portuguese trade routes after 1510. from there they spread into the rest of indian cooking over the following centuries. the cashew took root so successfully in goa's soil that it is now used to distill feni, the region's signature spirit. quick facts region west coast (goa) staple grain rice defining technique vinegar-based marination (portuguese-derived) key historical moment portuguese colonial rule, 1510 to 1961 signature dish vindaloo xacuti: a roasted-spice coconut curry, blending konkani technique with portuguese-era trade spices. bebinca: a rich, layered coconut-and-egg cake of portuguese-goan origin. signature dishes vindaloo : pork or meat marinated in vinegar, garlic, and chili; from the portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos . xacuti : a roasted-spice coconut curry. sorpotel : a tangy, spiced pork offal dish, a goan catholic specialty. bebinca : a layered coconut-egg dessert cake. goan fish curry rice : the everyday coastal staple, built on coconut and kokum.

entries.title: Gujarati Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Gujarati cuisine: Jain vegetarianism, maritime trade, and the sweet-salty-sour balance of the Gujarati thali.
entries.text: gujarati cuisine gujarati cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of gujarati cuisine: jain vegetarianism, maritime trade, and the sweet-salty-sour balance of the gujarati thali. gujarati cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana west india gujarati cuisine india's great vegetarian tradition, where sweet, salty, and sour are balanced deliberately on a single plate. trade, religion, and a coastline gujarat has been a maritime trading region since antiquity. lothal, one of the indus valley civilization's key port cities, sat on gujarat's coast, and the port of surat became one of the mughal empire's busiest trade hubs by the 17th century. that history brought early, sustained contact with outside ingredients and cultures. the more decisive influence on the cuisine, though, is religious. gujarat has one of india's largest jain populations, and jain dietary law prohibits root vegetables as well as meat, to avoid harming the organisms in the soil. that pushed the region toward one of the subcontinent's oldest and most disciplined vegetarian traditions. the sweet-salty-sour thali the defining trait of gujarati cooking, more than any single ingredient, is a deliberate balancing act. many savory dishes carry a small amount of sugar or jaggery alongside chili and tamarind or lemon, so a single dish, and a full thali, moves between sweet, salty, sour, and spicy rather than settling on one note. that is not inconsistency. it is a codified aesthetic, and one of the more instantly identifiable regional signatures in indian cooking, since most other regions treat sweetness strictly as a dessert category. a pinch of sugar in the dal isn't a mistake in gujarati cooking. it's the whole point. farsan, and food built for trade routes gujarat also produced one of india's richest snack-food traditions, known as farsan. these are steamed, fried, or fermented savory snacks like dhokla and khandvi, most built from besan (gram flour) or fermented rice-lentil batters. farsan developed partly as travel food for a historically mercantile, road-and-sea-trading population, favoring items that kept well and travelled easily. that same trading community, the gujarati and marwari merchant diaspora, later carried gujarati vegetarian food culture across india and eventually the world, making dishes like dhokla recognizable well outside the state. quick facts region western india (gujarat) staple grain wheat & millet (bajra, jowar), plus rice on the coast defining technique sweet-salty-sour balancing; steamed & fried gram-flour snacks (farsan) key historical influence jain vegetarianism & a long maritime trading history signature trait one of india's most strictly vegetarian regional cuisines dhokla: a steamed, fermented gram-flour cake. undhiyu: a slow-cooked mixed-vegetable dish, a surat winter specialty. signature dishes dhokla : a steamed, spongy, fermented gram-flour cake. khandvi : thin, rolled gram-flour and yogurt savory bites. undhiyu : a slow-cooked mix of winter vegetables, a surat specialty. thepla : a spiced flatbread, often made with fenugreek leaves. fafda-jalebi : crisp gram-flour strips paired with a syrup-soaked sweet, a classic weekend breakfast. gujarati kadhi : a mildly sweetened yogurt-and-gram-flour soup.

entries.title: Hyderabadi Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Hyderabadi cuisine: the Nizams' court kitchens, the Qutb Shahi dynasty, and the dum technique behind Hyderabadi biryani.
entries.text: hyderabadi cuisine hyderabadi cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of hyderabadi cuisine: the nizams' court kitchens, the qutb shahi dynasty, and the dum technique behind hyderabadi biryani. hyderabadi cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana the deccan hyderabadi cuisine persian court cooking met telugu spice tradition here. four centuries in the making, with one dish at the center of it all. two dynasties, one fusion cuisine hyderabadi cuisine is a fusion in the most literal sense. its history is unusually well documented because it grew up as a court cuisine, shaped deliberately by ruling dynasties rather than by agriculture and geography alone. the qutb shahi dynasty, which ruled the golconda sultanate from the 16th to 17th century, brought persian court cooking to the deccan. when the mughal empire later absorbed the region and the nizams (the asaf jahi dynasty) took power in the 18th century, their kitchens combined that persian-mughal foundation with the spice-forward telugu and marathwada cooking already established locally. the result is rich and fragrant on its persian-mughal side and sharply spiced on its deccan side. the dum technique what sets hyderabadi biryani apart from other indian biryanis is the cooking method rather than the spice blend. in the "kachi" (raw) style, marinated raw meat is layered directly with partially cooked rice. the pot is sealed and slow-cooked over low heat (dum), so the rice finishes cooking in the steam and juices the meat releases. the two are never cooked separately and combined afterward. this layering-and-sealing method, often done by sealing the lid with dough to trap steam, came from persian court kitchens. its survival in hyderabad is a direct trace of the nizams' persian-influenced cooks. the layering-and-sealing technique behind hyderabadi biryani is a 300-year-old persian court method, still practiced almost exactly as it was. haleem and the nizami table haleem, a dense, slow-pounded stew of wheat, lentils, and meat, has similarly deep roots. it traces back to arab and persian meat-and-wheat porridges (related to the middle eastern harees), brought into the nizams' kitchens and adapted with local spice. in hyderabad it is now tied closely to ramadan, served as an iftar dish across the city each evening during the fasting month. quick facts region deccan plateau (hyderabad, telangana) staple grain rice defining technique dum: sealed-pot, layered slow-cooking key historical influence qutb shahi & nizami (asaf jahi) court kitchens, 16th to 20th century signature dish hyderabadi biryani haleem: a slow-pounded wheat, lentil, and meat stew with roots in arab and persian cooking. qubani ka meetha: a stewed apricot dessert of persian dessert lineage, served with cream. signature dishes hyderabadi biryani : layered, dum-cooked rice and marinated meat. haleem : a slow-pounded wheat, lentil, and meat stew, a ramadan specialty. mirchi ka salan : a tangy chili curry in a peanut-sesame gravy. double ka meetha : a bread pudding fried and soaked in sweetened milk, of persian dessert lineage. qubani ka meetha : a stewed apricot dessert, served with cream.

entries.title: Kashmiri Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Kashmiri cuisine: Central Asian chefs brought by Timur, the wazwan feast, and the religious split between Kashmiri Pandit and Kashmiri Muslim cooking.
entries.text: kashmiri cuisine kashmiri cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of kashmiri cuisine: central asian chefs brought by timur, the wazwan feast, and the religious split between kashmiri pandit and kashmiri muslim cooking. kashmiri cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana himalayan north kashmiri cuisine a persian-inflected court cuisine grafted onto a himalayan valley, built around a feast that treats meat as ceremony rather than ingredient. a central asian graft onto a himalayan valley kashmiri cooking's most distinctive institution, the wazwan feast, doesn't trace back to the rest of the indian subcontinent at all. its roots are usually placed in the late 14th century, when timur's invasion of kashmir brought central asian and persian cooks, the wazas, into the valley. over the following centuries, under later sultanate and mughal-era patronage, that imported tradition merged with local ingredients (saffron, lotus stem, local lamb). what emerged was no longer quite persian, and no longer quite anything else on the subcontinent either. the wazwan: a feast measured in courses, not dishes a full wazwan traditionally runs to around 36 courses. a team of wazas prepares it, led by a head chef called the vaste waza, and it is served family-style on a single large platter called a trami, four diners to a plate. you cook it for weddings and major occasions rather than ordering it off a menu, and the meal builds toward a defined climax instead of just presenting dishes in sequence. the wazwan's final course is always the same dish: gushtaba, pounded meatballs in a white yogurt gravy. its arrival signals that the feast is over. two kashmiri cuisines, split by religion as in goa and rajasthan, one regional label covers two distinct culinary traditions here, split along religious lines. kashmiri pandit (hindu) cooking avoids onion and garlic on religious grounds and builds its pungency instead from asafoetida (hing) and dried ginger powder (saunth), producing dishes like a pale, tangy pandit-style yakhni. kashmiri muslim cooking, the tradition behind the wazwan, leans heavily on onion and garlic and produces the deep-red rogan josh most outsiders associate with the region. same valley, same core ingredients, genuinely different everyday cooking. saffron, and the valley's one true luxury crop the fields around pampore, near srinagar, are one of the very few places on earth where saffron is grown commercially, and kashmir treats it accordingly. it is a defining flavor here rather than a garnish, turning up in modur pulav (sweet saffron rice) and in desserts. above all it goes into kahwa, a green tea steeped with saffron, cardamom, and almonds and served without milk. that makes it a genuinely different drink from the milk-based chai found almost everywhere else in india. quick facts region kashmir valley (himalayan north) staple grain rice defining technique slow-cooked meat, hand-pounded for hours key historical moment central asian wazas arriving with timur's 14th-century invasion signature dish rogan josh modur pulav: sweet saffron rice studded with dried fruit and nuts. dum aloo: baby potatoes slow-cooked in a spiced, deep-red gravy. signature dishes rogan josh : lamb cooked in oil at high heat, colored deep red by kashmiri chili or, traditionally, ratan jot (cockscomb flower) rather than tomato. yakhni : a yogurt-based curry cooked with whole spices; the pandit version omits onion, garlic, turmeric, and chili entirely. gushtaba : hand-pounded meatballs in white yogurt gravy, the ceremonial final course of the wazwan. modur pulav : sweet saffron rice with dried fruit, milk, and sugar. kahwa : green tea with saffron, cardamom, and almonds, served without milk.

entries.title: Kerala Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Kerala cuisine: the Malabar spice trade that drew Rome, Arabia, China, and Europe to one coastline, coconut as the region's defining fat, and the Onam sadya feast.
entries.text: kerala cuisine kerala cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of kerala cuisine: the malabar spice trade that drew rome, arabia, china, and europe to one coastline, coconut as the region's defining fat, and the onam sadya feast. kerala cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana malabar coast kerala cuisine the coastline that drew rome, arabia, china, and europe in search of a single spice, built around coconut instead of ghee and a religious diversity few other regions can match. the coast the whole world sailed for kerala's food history starts with a fact that's easy to underrate. for close to two thousand years, the malabar coast was the world's main source of black pepper, valuable enough to draw roman traders, arab merchants, and chinese fleets to the same stretch of coastline long before the mughals ever set foot in india. that trade reached its best-known turning point in 1498, when vasco da gama landed at kozhikode (calicut) in search of pepper. his voyage opened a direct european sea route to india, and with it over a century of portuguese and later dutch and british competition for the spice trade. kerala did not merely take part in that history. for a very long time, it was the reason for it. three communities, one coastline centuries of trade left kerala with a religious and culinary diversity that's unusual even within india. kochi has hosted a jewish community since roughly the time of the spice trade's earliest centuries. arab traders left behind the mappila muslim community of the malabar coast, whose thalassery biryani, built on a small-grained khyma rice rather than basmati, is genuinely distinct from both the hyderabadi and awadhi versions. and kerala's syrian christian community, tracing its roots to some of the oldest christian communities outside the middle east, contributes rich, dark meat dishes like duck roast and beef fry that sit alongside an otherwise heavily vegetarian hindu tradition. vasco da gama didn't sail to india in general. he sailed to kozhikode, specifically for kerala's pepper. coconut, not ghee, as the defining fat where punjabi or awadhi cooking runs on ghee and dairy, kerala's kitchens run on coconut in nearly every form at once. coconut oil handles the frying and tempering, thick coconut milk finishes a curry, and fresh grated coconut goes straight into chutneys and vegetable dishes. it suits a tropical, coastal climate, and it is the single clearest thing separating kerala's cooking from its northern neighbors and even from much of the rest of south india. a vegetarian feast from a state famous for its beef kerala is one of the few indian states, alongside goa and the northeast, where beef is commonly and openly eaten, mostly among its large christian and muslim communities. that makes the sadya, kerala's traditional festival feast, a striking contrast. it is an entirely vegetarian meal of around twenty to twenty-six dishes, served in a fixed arrangement on a banana leaf and eaten by hand. it is central to onam and other major celebrations, whatever a household eats the rest of the year. the sadya is less a dinner than a piece of shared choreography, right down to the order in which dishes are mixed into the rice. quick facts region malabar coast, southwest india staple grain rice defining technique coconut oil, milk, and grated coconut used in nearly every dish key historical moment centuries at the center of the global pepper trade, culminating in vasco da gama's 1498 landing at calicut signature dish fish curry meen curry: fish simmered in a tangy, coconut-and-kokum gravy, traditionally cooked in a clay pot. appam with duck curry: a lacy, fermented rice pancake paired with a rich syrian christian specialty. signature dishes meen curry (fish curry) : fish simmered in a tangy coconut gravy, often soured with kokum. appam : a fermented rice-and-coconut pancake, lacy and thin at the edges, thick in the center. sadya : a roughly 20-to-26-dish vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf for onam and other celebrations. thalassery biryani : a mappila muslim biryani made with small-grained khyma rice rather than basmati. duck roast : a rich, dark, spice-heavy dish from kerala's syrian christian tradition.

entries.title: Maharashtrian Cuisine
entries.snippet: How geography split Maharashtrian cuisine into a coastal Konkan tradition and a spicy Deccan one, and how vada pav was invented for Mumbai's mill workers.
entries.text: maharashtrian cuisine maharashtrian cuisine: history & iconic dishes how geography split maharashtrian cuisine into a coastal konkan tradition and a spicy deccan one, and how vada pav was invented for mumbai's mill workers. maharashtrian cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana west india maharashtrian cuisine a coastal tradition and a plateau tradition, sharing one state, plus the street food that fed mumbai's mill workers. konkan coast vs. deccan plateau maharashtra's cuisine really splits into two distinct traditions defined by geography. along the konkan coast, the food looks a lot like its coastal neighbors goa and kerala: rice, coconut, and seafood, cooked with kokum (a tart dried fruit) for sourness. inland, on the drier deccan plateau, the cuisine shifts to millets (jowar and bajra) instead of rice, peanuts and sesame instead of coconut, and famously dry, intensely spiced curries. kolhapuri cuisine, from the southern deccan, is often cited as one of the spiciest regional styles in india. the maratha empire and a warrior food culture maharashtra's political identity is inseparable from the maratha empire, built under chhatrapati shivaji in the 17th century and expanding into one of the dominant powers in india by the 18th. foods tied to military campaigns had to be practical, portable, and high in energy. dry chutneys, spice mixes like goda masala and kanda-lasun masala, and preserved pickles all fit that need. they stayed in everyday cooking long after the campaigns ended. vada pav wasn't handed down through generations. it was invented on a specific street corner, for a specific economic reason, in 1966. mumbai and the invention of vada pav the most-told food-history story from this region is a recent, well-documented one. vada pav, a spiced potato fritter in a bread roll, is credited to a street vendor named ashok vaidya, who began selling it near dadar railway station in 1966. it was explicitly designed as a cheap, fast, filling meal for mumbai's textile mill workers, at a time when western-style sandwiches were priced out of reach for that same crowd. it's a rare case in indian food history where a genuinely "invented" dish, rather than one that gradually evolved, can be traced to a specific person, place, and year. it went on to become mumbai's defining street food. quick facts region western india (maharashtra): coastal konkan & inland deccan staple grain rice (coastal), jowar & bajra millets (inland) defining technique coconut-and-kokum coastal cooking; dry, intense deccan spice blends key historical moment vada pav's invention near dadar station, mumbai, 1966 signature dish vada pav misal pav: a spicy sprouted-lentil curry topped with farsan, served with bread. modak: a steamed rice-flour dumpling filled with coconut and jaggery. signature dishes vada pav : a spiced potato fritter in a bread roll, invented in mumbai in 1966. misal pav : a spicy sprouted-lentil curry topped with crunchy farsan, served with bread. puran poli : a sweet flatbread stuffed with a jaggery-lentil filling. modak : a steamed dumpling of rice flour, coconut, and jaggery, associated with the ganesh chaturthi festival. kolhapuri mutton : an intensely spiced, dry-roasted-masala curry from the southern deccan.

entries.title: Northeast Indian Cuisine
entries.snippet: How isolation from the mainland gave India's eight northeastern states a cuisine built on fermentation and smoking rather than garam masala and dairy.
entries.text: northeast indian cuisine northeast indian cuisine: history & iconic dishes how isolation from the mainland gave india's eight northeastern states a cuisine built on fermentation and smoking rather than garam masala and dairy. northeast indian cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana eight states northeast indian cuisine not one cuisine but eight, connected less to mainland indian cooking than to the fermentation and bamboo traditions of tibet and southeast asia across the border. not one cuisine, but eight "northeast indian" is a geographic label, not a culinary one. it covers assam, arunachal pradesh, manipur, meghalaya, mizoram, nagaland, tripura, and sikkim. that's eight states, dozens of distinct tribal and ethnic groups, and about as many genuinely different food traditions. they don't share a spice blend the way punjabi or hyderabadi cooking does. what they share is an approach. flavor comes from fermentation and smoking rather than a stacked masala, and the staples are rice and local greens rather than wheat and dairy. geography is a large part of why. the region connects to the rest of india only through the narrow siliguri corridor, sometimes called the "chicken's neck," while sharing long borders with tibet, myanmar, bhutan, and bangladesh. historically, trade and cultural exchange across those borders shaped the region's kitchens at least as much as anything arriving from delhi. fermentation as the region's spice rack where a punjabi or hyderabadi kitchen reaches for a garam masala blend, much of the northeast reaches for something fermented instead. bamboo shoot, fresh, dried, or fermented into a sour paste known as soibum in manipur or khorisa in assam, shows up across the region as a souring, funky base note. naga cooking in particular relies on akhuni (also spelled axone), fermented soybean with a pungency often compared to japanese natto, worked into pork and chicken dishes as the primary flavor driver rather than a background ingredient. bhut jolokia, the "ghost pepper" grown in assam and nagaland, held the guinness world record for hottest chili in the world from 2007 to 2011, and the indian army has tested it in smoke grenades. smoke, not cream, as the flavor base the region's meat cooking, especially pork, leans heavily on open-fire smoking rather than the dairy-rich gravies common further west and north; there's comparatively little use of cream, ghee, or yogurt as a curry base. assamese cooking adds its own signatures on top of this. masor tenga is a light, sour fish curry soured with tomato or lemon rather than tamarind. khar is built on an alkaline water filtered through banana-peel ash, a flavor and technique with no real parallel elsewhere in indian cooking. quick facts region eight northeastern states staple grain rice defining technique fermentation and smoking, not dairy-based gravies key historical moment geographic isolation via the siliguri corridor; closer historical trade ties to tibet and southeast asia than to mainland india signature dish smoked pork with bamboo shoot (naga) naga-style smoked pork ribs with bamboo shoot, a signature combination across nagaland. momos: a tibetan import that became a northeast and himalayan-india staple. signature dishes axone pork (nagaland): pork cooked with fermented soybean, one of the region's most distinctive flavor combinations. masor tenga (assam): a light, sour fish curry soured with tomato or lemon. khar (assam): a savory dish built on alkaline water filtered through banana-peel ash. bamboo shoot pickle : fermented or fresh bamboo shoot, used across nearly every state in the region. momos and thukpa (sikkim, arunachal pradesh): tibetan-influenced dumplings and noodle soup, staples in the himalayan-border states.

entries.title: Odia Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Odia (Odisha) cuisine: rice and pakhala, the giant temple kitchen at Puri, and the rasgulla that Odisha and Bengal both claim.
entries.text: odia cuisine odia cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of odia (odisha) cuisine: rice and pakhala, the giant temple kitchen at puri, and the rasgulla that odisha and bengal both claim. odia cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana east india odia cuisine a rice, mustard, and temple cuisine on the bay of bengal, lighter and less oily than its better-known neighbor. rice, the coast, and a lot of restraint odisha sits on the bay of bengal, between bengal to the northeast and the telugu south. its food shares plenty with bengali cooking: rice as the staple, mustard, freshwater fish, and a serious sweet tradition. but it pulls back on all of them. odia cooking is usually lighter, less oily, and more gently spiced than the food on either side of it. the everyday tempering is pancha phutana , a five-spice mix of mustard, cumin, fennel, fenugreek, and nigella seeds. the dish that sums up the cuisine is pakhala. in the heat of an odia summer, a common lunch is rice left to ferment overnight in water, served cool with salt, a little yogurt, and fried or mashed vegetables on the side. it cools the body and uses up the previous day's rice. odisha even marks a pakhala dibasa (pakhala day) every 20 march. the kitchen at the jagannath temple the biggest influence on odia food is the temple, not a royal court. at the jagannath temple in puri, the kitchen (the rosaghara) is one of the largest in the world and cooks for thousands of pilgrims a day. food is made in earthen pots stacked several high over wood fires, and by tradition the pot on top cooks first. what is offered to the deity is the mahaprasada, dozens of dishes known together as the chhappan bhoga, or "fifty-six offerings." it is all vegetarian and cooked without onion, garlic, tomato, or chili. once offered, it is sold and eaten side by side by pilgrims of every background at the ananda bazaar next to the temple. that plain, satvik, rice-and-dal cooking shaped a lot of odia home food too. in odisha the defining kitchen isn't a court or a restaurant. it's a temple that has cooked for pilgrims the same way for centuries. who really invented the rasgulla? odisha and bengal have argued for years over who created the rasgulla (rasagola). odisha's version, the pahala rasagola, is tied to the jagannath temple, where a chhena sweet has long been offered to the deities. bengal traces its rosogolla to the kolkata confectioner nobin chandra das in the 1860s. the dispute reached india's geographical indication (gi) system. odisha won a gi tag for "odisha rasagola" in 2019, two years after west bengal secured one for "banglar rosogolla." the tags recognize two regional versions rather than settling who was first. odisha's other signature sweet is chhena poda, or "burnt cheese," a baked block of fresh chhena and sugar with a caramelized crust, usually traced to the town of nayagarh. a coastline of its own along the coast, sea fish and prawns do the work that river fish does inland. dishes like chungudi malai, prawns in a mild coconut-milk gravy, point to odisha's long shoreline and its old sea trade with southeast asia. the state still marks that seafaring past every year at bali jatra, a festival in cuttack that remembers ancient voyages to bali and beyond. quick facts region odisha (formerly orissa), east coast staple grain rice defining technique earthen-pot temple cooking; pancha phutana five-spice; mustard and chhena sweets key site the jagannath temple kitchen at puri signature protein freshwater and sea fish, prawns chhena poda: a baked block of fresh chhena and sugar with a caramelized crust. pakhala: rice fermented overnight in water, served cool through the odia summer. signature dishes dalma : lentils cooked with vegetables and tempered with pancha phutana, a temple and everyday staple. pakhala : rice soaked or fermented in water, eaten cool with simple sides. macha besara : fish in a mustard-and-garlic gravy. chungudi malai : prawns in a mild coconut-milk curry. santula : a light, gently spiced mix of steamed vegetables. chhena poda : baked "burnt cheese" sweet with a caramelized crust. rasagola (pahala) : chhena balls in syrup, the temple-linked odia version.

entries.title: Punjabi Cuisine
entries.snippet: How the tandoor and Punjab's wheat belt shaped its cuisine, and how Partition-era refugees invented butter chicken in Delhi.
entries.text: punjabi cuisine punjabi cuisine: history & iconic dishes how the tandoor and punjab's wheat belt shaped its cuisine, and how partition-era refugees invented butter chicken in delhi. punjabi cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana north india punjabi cuisine tandoors, wheat, and dairy, plus the refugee kitchens of 1947 that turned punjabi food into india's most recognized export. the land of five rivers punjab takes its name from panj āb (five rivers), and that geography built the cuisine long before any dynasty or border did. the indus plain is some of the most fertile farmland in south asia, and for centuries it has produced wheat rather than rice as its staple grain, along with the dairy that comes naturally with extensive cattle and buffalo farming. roti, paratha, naan, ghee, makkhan (butter), lassi, paneer. the core of punjabi cooking is really the core of punjabi agriculture. the tandoor, the clay oven now inseparable from punjabi food, isn't originally punjabi at all. it arrived with central asian and mughal influence, likely by the 16th century. what punjab did was make it central. tandoori roti, naan, and tandoor-roasted meats became the backbone of a cooking style built around live fire and dairy-based marinades. 1947, and the invention of "indian restaurant food" the single biggest turning point in punjabi cuisine's history isn't ancient. it's 1947. partition displaced millions of punjabis from what became west punjab, pakistan, and a large number resettled in delhi. among them were restaurateurs who rebuilt their trade from scratch, and it's this generation that is widely credited with inventing what most of the world now thinks of as "indian food." butter chicken is the clearest example. the story, credited to kundan lal gujral of delhi's moti mahal restaurant, is that leftover tandoori chicken was simmered in a tomato-butter gravy to keep it from drying out. that practical fix became a signature dish. dal makhani, black lentils finished the same way with butter and cream, followed the same logic. both dishes are, in culinary-history terms, remarkably recent. they're refugee-kitchen inventions from the late 1940s that went on to define an entire cuisine's global reputation. roti and dairy built the everyday punjabi table. a generation of refugee restaurateurs in 1940s delhi built the version the rest of the world knows. village food vs. restaurant food it's worth separating the two punjabi cuisines that coexist today. one is the everyday rural table. sarson da saag (mustard greens, slow-cooked with spices) eaten with makki di roti (cornmeal flatbread), along with simple dals, buttermilk, and pickles, food built for farming families and cold punjab winters. the other is the richer, dairy-heavy restaurant repertoire of butter chicken, dal makhani, and paneer dishes, built for the diaspora and now exported worldwide. both are authentically punjabi. they just come from different centuries and different kitchens. quick facts region north india (punjab, extending into delhi & the diaspora) staple grain wheat defining technique tandoor (clay oven) cooking key historical moment partition, 1947: refugee restaurateurs in delhi signature fat ghee & butter butter chicken: invented at delhi's moti mahal in the late 1940s. chole bhature: spiced chickpeas with deep-fried leavened bread. signature dishes butter chicken : tandoori chicken simmered in a tomato, butter, and cream gravy. dal makhani : black lentils and kidney beans, slow-cooked with butter and cream. sarson da saag & makki di roti : mustard greens with cornmeal flatbread, a winter staple. chole bhature : spiced chickpea curry with fried bread, a delhi-punjabi street food classic. amritsari kulcha : stuffed leavened flatbread from amritsar, baked in a tandoor. lassi : a churned yogurt drink, sweet or salted.

entries.title: Rajasthani Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Rajasthani cuisine: desert cooking, Rajput royal kitchens, and the Marwari vegetarian tradition.
entries.text: rajasthani cuisine rajasthani cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of rajasthani cuisine: desert cooking, rajput royal kitchens, and the marwari vegetarian tradition. rajasthani cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana northwest india rajasthani cuisine cooking adapted to the desert, built around scarce water and ingredients that keep. two very different food traditions grew up inside it. cooking for the thar desert much of rajasthan sits within or on the edge of the thar desert, and the cuisine answers to that environment more directly than almost any other indian regional tradition. fresh vegetables were historically scarce and water was precious. so the cooking developed around ingredients that could survive drought and long storage. these were dried lentils and beans, dried desert berries and pods such as ker and sangri (gathered from native desert shrubs), buttermilk and other dairy standing in for fresh produce, and plenty of ghee to add richness where fresh ingredients couldn't. two traditions, one region rajasthan's food history carries a real internal split. on one side is the rajput tradition, the warrior-noble class whose royal kitchens grew out of hunting culture and historically included game and meat. laal maas ("red meat"), a fiery mutton curry tied to royal rajput feasts, is the clearest surviving example. on the other side is the marwari tradition, rajasthan's major merchant community, historically jain or vaishnav hindu, and strictly vegetarian. the marwari community's trading networks reached across india, and they carried rajasthani vegetarian food far beyond the state's borders, including what's now sold across the country as "rajasthani thali." a royal hunting curry and a merchant caste's strict vegetarianism grew up in the same desert, and both are equally "rajasthani." dal baati churma: a meal engineered for storage the state's signature dish shows how the whole cuisine works. baati are hard wheat-flour rolls, traditionally baked (originally in embers) until dense and dry. it's a bread built to last rather than to be eaten fresh and soft. they're served crushed into ghee alongside dal (lentils) and churma (a sweet, crumbled wheat-and-jaggery mixture). every part of the dish is built for a hot, dry climate and for keeping without refrigeration, and that idea runs through nearly the whole cuisine. quick facts region northwest india (rajasthan, including the thar desert) staple grain wheat, millet (bajra) defining technique preservation-first cooking: dried lentils, dairy, minimal fresh water/vegetables key historical split rajput (royal, meat-eating) vs. marwari (merchant, strictly vegetarian) signature fat ghee a rajasthani thali: the marwari vegetarian tradition, carried nationwide by the merchant diaspora. kachori: a deep-fried, spiced-lentil-stuffed pastry. signature dishes dal baati churma : hard wheat rolls with lentils and a sweet crumbled wheat dish. laal maas : a fiery, red-chili mutton curry from the rajput royal tradition. gatte ki sabzi : gram-flour dumplings in a spiced yogurt gravy, a classic "no fresh vegetables needed" dish. ker sangri : a dish of dried desert berries and beans, unique to the region. kachori : a deep-fried pastry stuffed with spiced lentils or onions.

entries.title: South Indian Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of South Indian cuisine: rice, fermentation, and how chili peppers from the Americas transformed Andhra cooking.
entries.text: south indian cuisine south indian cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of south indian cuisine: rice, fermentation, and how chili peppers from the americas transformed andhra cooking. south indian cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana south india south indian cuisine rice, lentils, and fermentation. four distinct food traditions built on the same ancient staples. four cuisines, one umbrella term "south indian food" is a handy shorthand, but it flattens four genuinely distinct traditions: tamil, kerala (malayali), karnataka (kannadiga), and andhra/telangana (telugu). they share a common base of rice as the staple grain, lentils for protein, and a reliance on fermentation and tempering (tadka, or whole spices bloomed in hot oil). but they diverge sharply in heat, fat, and flavor. kerala leans on coconut oil and coconut milk. andhra is famous even within india for being the spiciest of the major regional cuisines. tamil nadu's chettinad region built its own tradition around dry-roasted whole spices. an old fermentation tradition the dosa and idli are now the most globally recognized south indian foods, and both rest on an old technique. you soak and grind rice and urad dal (black gram), then let the batter ferment overnight before cooking. the fermentation develops flavor and also makes the batter's nutrients easier to digest. references to dosa-like foods appear in tamil and kannada literature going back over a thousand years. that makes it one of the older cooking techniques still in continuous use on the subcontinent, well before chilies, tomatoes, or potatoes arrived. rice, lentils, and fermentation are the old core. chili heat, now andhra's calling card, is a 16th-century import. the chili pepper's arrival chili peppers are not native to india at all, one of the most-quoted facts of indian food history. they arrived via portuguese trade routes after 1498, part of the broader "columbian exchange" that moved new world crops into asia. before then, heat in south indian cooking came from black pepper (a native kerala export that drove centuries of spice-trade interest from rome to europe) and from ginger. chilies caught on fast, nowhere more than in andhra pradesh, whose cuisine is now defined by a level of heat that postdates the mughal empire itself. coffee, coconuts, and the meal as a system the south indian thali (or "meals," as it's often called in tamil nadu and karnataka) follows a plan. rice is the anchor, with sambar, rasam, kootu, and chutneys eaten in a set order, usually finishing with yogurt rice to cool the palate. it's typically served on a banana leaf. filter coffee, brewed with a metal filter and served with frothed milk, became a south indian institution in the 19th and 20th centuries. it remains as culturally central as the dosa itself. quick facts region tamil nadu, kerala, karnataka, andhra pradesh & telangana staple grain rice defining technique batter fermentation & oil tempering (tadka) key historical moment post-1498 arrival of the chili pepper via portuguese trade signature fat coconut oil (kerala/coastal tn), sesame & groundnut oil elsewhere idli and sambar: steamed fermented rice cakes with a tamarind lentil stew. sambar: a tamarind-based lentil stew that anchors the south indian thali. signature dishes dosa : a fermented rice-and-lentil crepe, often filled with spiced potato (masala dosa). idli : steamed fermented rice cakes, typically eaten with sambar and chutney. sambar : a tamarind-based lentil and vegetable stew. rasam : a thin, peppery tamarind soup, often served after sambar. uttapam : a thicker, savory pancake made from the same fermented batter as dosa. filter coffee : south india's defining beverage tradition.

entries.title: Awadhi Kheer
entries.snippet: slow-reduced rice pudding scented with saffron, cardamom and a drop of kewra
entries.text: awadhi kheer awadhi/lucknowi slow-reduced rice pudding scented with saffron, cardamom and a drop of kewra vegetarian gluten-free no-onion-garlic milk basmati rice sugar ghee green cardamom saffron almonds pistachios raisins (kishmish) kewra water rub the pan with ghee, pour in the milk and bring it to a boil over medium heat, stirring. add the drained, crushed rice and lower the heat so the milk simmers gently. cook uncovered 45–50 minutes, stirring and scraping the base every 4–5 minutes, until the rice is soft and the milk has reduced by nearly half. push the cream that forms on the sides back into the pan as you go. add the sugar and stir 8 minutes until it dissolves and the kheer thickens again. stir in the saffron milk and cook 4 minutes until the colour is even. add the cardamom powder, almonds, pistachios and raisins and cook 2 minutes. take off the heat, stir in the kewra water, and let it stand 15 minutes. serve warm, or chill 2 hours and serve cold with extra slivered pistachios.

entries.title: Awadhi Murgh Masala
entries.snippet: everyday bone-in chicken curry, browned onion and yogurt with ground cashew, gentle on chilli
entries.text: awadhi murgh masala awadhi/lucknowi everyday bone-in chicken curry, browned onion and yogurt with ground cashew, gentle on chilli gluten-free chicken yogurt / dahi onion cashews ghee ginger garlic tomato coriander powder cumin powder (jeera) kashmiri chilli powder turmeric powder garam masala green cardamom cloves cinnamon bay leaf kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves) coriander leaves (cilantro) water salt heat the ghee, add the bay leaf, cardamom, cloves and cinnamon and let them swell for 30 seconds. add the sliced onion and cook over medium heat, stirring, until deep golden brown, 12–14 minutes. stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 2 minutes until the raw smell goes. add the coriander powder, cumin powder, kashmiri chilli and 2 tbsp water and bhuno 2 minutes. add the chopped tomato, if using, and cook until it breaks down completely, 4 minutes. lower the flame, add the marinated chicken with all its yogurt and stir constantly for 8 minutes until the fat separates and the pieces are coated. blend the soaked cashews with 4 tbsp water to a smooth paste and stir it in with the salt. pour in 300ml warm water, cover and simmer 18–20 minutes until the chicken is tender and the gravy has thickened. uncover, add the garam masala and crushed kasuri methi and reduce 3 minutes. rest covered 5 minutes, scatter with coriander leaves and serve with paratha or rice.

entries.title: Awadhi Paneer Korma
entries.snippet: paneer in an ivory cashew and yogurt gravy, mild and heavily perfumed
entries.text: awadhi paneer korma awadhi/lucknowi paneer in an ivory cashew and yogurt gravy, mild and heavily perfumed vegetarian gluten-free paneer yogurt / dahi onion cashews melon seeds (magaz) ghee cream ginger garlic green chilli coriander powder fennel powder green cardamom mace (javitri) white pepper saffron kewra water water salt fry the sliced onion in 2 tbsp ghee over medium heat until pale gold and soft, 8 minutes. do not let it brown. cool the onion and grind it with the soaked cashews, melon seeds and 4 tbsp water to a completely smooth paste. heat the remaining 2 tbsp ghee, add the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 90 seconds until the raw edge is gone. add the onion-cashew paste and cook on low for 6 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens and no longer smells raw. take the pan off the heat and whisk in the yogurt in three additions, then return to the lowest flame for 5 minutes until the ghee shows at the edges. stir in the coriander powder, fennel powder, mace, white pepper, green chillies and salt and cook 2 minutes. add 250ml warm water and simmer uncovered 6 minutes until the gravy coats a spoon. drain the paneer, slip it in and simmer 4 minutes only. finish with cream, cardamom powder, saffron milk and a few drops of kewra water. rest covered 5 minutes before serving.

entries.title: Boti Kebab
entries.snippet: yogurt-marinated mutton cubes, charred outside and juicy through
entries.text: boti kebab awadhi/lucknowi yogurt-marinated mutton cubes, charred outside and juicy through gluten-free nut-free mutton / lamb yogurt / dahi raw green papaya ginger garlic kashmiri chilli powder coriander powder garam masala black pepper mustard oil besan (gram flour) ghee lemon / lime chaat masala salt pat the mutton cubes completely dry and prick each one two or three times with a fork. rub in the papaya paste, ginger, garlic and salt and leave 20 minutes. whisk the hung yogurt with the roasted besan, kashmiri chilli, coriander powder, garam masala, black pepper and the cooled mustard oil until smooth. fold the meat through the marinade, cover and refrigerate overnight. thread onto skewers with a finger gap between cubes so the heat gets all the way round. grill over medium-hot charcoal or under an oven grill at 240c for 12–15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes. baste with ghee in the last 4 minutes and let the edges blacken in patches. rest 3 minutes off the heat, then dust with chaat masala and squeeze over lemon.

entries.title: Dum Aloo Lucknowi
entries.snippet: fried baby potatoes finished in a yogurt gravy with fennel and dry ginger, no onion or garlic
entries.text: dum aloo lucknowi awadhi/lucknowi fried baby potatoes finished in a yogurt gravy with fennel and dry ginger, no onion or garlic vegetarian gluten-free no-onion-garlic nut-free potato yogurt / dahi ghee neutral oil asafoetida (hing) fennel powder dry ginger powder (saunth) coriander powder kashmiri chilli powder turmeric powder cumin seeds green cardamom cloves cinnamon bay leaf garam masala kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves) water salt prick the boiled, peeled potatoes deeply all over and pat them dry. deep fry them in hot oil until golden and lightly blistered, 4–5 minutes. drain and set aside. whisk the yogurt with the coriander powder, kashmiri chilli, turmeric, fennel powder and dry ginger powder to a smooth, lump-free mix. heat the ghee in a kadhai, add the bay leaf, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and cumin seeds and let them crackle 30 seconds. add the asafoetida, count to five, then immediately pour in the spiced yogurt. cook on the lowest flame, stirring without stopping, for 7–8 minutes until the mixture thickens and the ghee separates. add the fried potatoes and salt and turn them through the masala for 3 minutes. pour in 250ml warm water, bring to a simmer, then cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes. uncover, stir in the garam masala and crushed kasuri methi and reduce 3 minutes until the gravy clings to the potatoes. rest covered 5 minutes before serving with sheermal or plain rice.

entries.title: Galouti Kebab
entries.snippet: Minced mutton kebabs so soft they collapse on the tongue, from the Nawab's kitchen
entries.text: galouti kebab awadhi/lucknowi minced mutton kebabs so soft they collapse on the tongue, from the nawab's kitchen gluten-free mutton / lamb raw green papaya ghee onion cashews garam masala mace (javitri) nutmeg green cardamom ginger garlic saffron besan (gram flour) salt blend the mince to a smooth paste with the papaya, ginger and garlic. rest 45 minutes, refrigerated. fry the sliced onion in ghee until deep brown, drain, cool and crush to a powder. this birista carries most of the sweetness. work the birista, ground cashew, garam masala, mace, nutmeg, cardamom, saffron milk and salt into the mince. it should be soft but hold a shape; add the roasted besan only if it will not. chill the mix 30 minutes, then shape into flat discs about 6cm across and 1cm thick. fry on a tawa in ghee over low-medium heat, 3-4 minutes a side. turn once and gently — they are fragile. serve immediately with ulte tawe ka paratha or plain sheermal.

entries.title: Kakori Kebab
entries.snippet: silky skewered mutton mince, perfumed with mace and khoya, that barely holds its shape
entries.text: kakori kebab awadhi/lucknowi silky skewered mutton mince, perfumed with mace and khoya, that barely holds its shape gluten-free mutton / lamb raw green papaya onion ghee khoya / mawa cashews almonds poppy seeds (khus khus) ginger garlic mace (javitri) nutmeg green cardamom white pepper garam masala saffron kewra water salt fry the sliced onion in 3 tbsp ghee over medium heat until evenly deep brown, 10–12 minutes. drain, cool until crisp, then crush to a powder. blend the mince with the papaya paste, ginger and garlic to a smooth, almost creamy paste. work in the birista powder, ground cashew, almond, poppy seed, khoya, mace, nutmeg, cardamom, white pepper, garam masala, saffron milk, kewra and salt. cover and refrigerate 2 hours, then chill in the freezer 15 minutes just before shaping. wet your palm and press the mince along a flat skewer in a sausage about 15cm long and 2cm thick, tapering the ends. grill over medium charcoal or in an oven at 220c, turning every 3 minutes and basting with ghee, for 12–15 minutes total. finish 1 minute directly over high heat to colour the outside. slide off the skewer, rest 2 minutes, and serve with sheermal and onion rings.

entries.title: Lucknowi Dum Biryani
entries.snippet: Pakki biryani: meat and rice cooked separately, then sealed and finished on dum
entries.text: lucknowi dum biryani awadhi/lucknowi pakki biryani: meat and rice cooked separately, then sealed and finished on dum gluten-free nut-free mutton / lamb basmati rice yogurt / dahi onion ginger garlic saffron green cardamom black cardamom cinnamon cloves bay leaf mace (javitri) kewra water mint ghee atta (wholewheat flour) salt cook the mutton with yogurt, ginger, garlic, half the birista, the whole spices and salt until tender and almost dry, about 45 minutes. this is the korma base. boil the soaked rice in heavily salted water with a bay leaf until it is 70% done — the grain should still have a firm core when pressed. layer: meat at the bottom, rice over it, then the saffron milk, remaining birista, mint, kewra and ghee across the top. seal the lid with a rope of atta dough, or cover tightly with foil and a lid. cook on the lowest possible heat for 25 minutes — over a tawa if your burner runs hot — or in a 160c oven. rest 10 minutes before breaking the seal, then lift from the bottom with a flat spoon so the grains stay whole.

entries.title: Murgh Korma
entries.snippet: pale, fragrant chicken in a yogurt and cashew gravy with no chilli heat to speak of
entries.text: murgh korma awadhi/lucknowi pale, fragrant chicken in a yogurt and cashew gravy with no chilli heat to speak of gluten-free chicken yogurt / dahi onion cashews almonds ghee ginger garlic coriander powder fennel powder green cardamom cloves cinnamon bay leaf mace (javitri) white pepper saffron kewra water water salt fry two sliced onions in 3 tbsp ghee over medium heat until evenly brown, 10–12 minutes. drain and reserve the birista. grind the soaked cashews, almonds and half the birista to a smooth paste with 4 tbsp water. in the same ghee add the remaining ghee, bay leaf, cardamom, cloves and cinnamon and let them swell for 30 seconds. add the third sliced onion and cook gently until soft and pale gold, 6 minutes, without letting it colour further. stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 2 minutes until the raw smell lifts. add the chicken and turn it in the masala over medium heat for 5 minutes, until it turns opaque but takes no colour. take the pan off the heat, stir in the whisked yogurt in three additions, then return to the lowest flame and cook 6–8 minutes, stirring constantly, until the fat separates. stir in the nut paste, coriander powder, fennel powder, mace, white pepper and salt and cook 4 minutes. pour in 300ml warm water, cover and simmer very gently 20–25 minutes until the chicken is tender. finish with the saffron milk, kewra water and the remaining birista crushed over the top. rest covered 10 minutes before serving.

entries.title: Mutton Korma
entries.snippet: slow-braised mutton in a dark, nut-thickened yogurt gravy scented with black cardamom
entries.text: mutton korma awadhi/lucknowi slow-braised mutton in a dark, nut-thickened yogurt gravy scented with black cardamom gluten-free mutton / lamb yogurt / dahi onion ghee cashews melon seeds (magaz) poppy seeds (khus khus) ginger garlic coriander powder kashmiri chilli powder black cardamom green cardamom cloves cinnamon bay leaf mace (javitri) nutmeg saffron kewra water water salt fry the sliced onions in 4 tbsp ghee over medium heat until deep brown, 12–14 minutes. drain the birista and reserve the ghee. grind the soaked seeds and nuts with two-thirds of the birista and 5 tbsp water to a smooth paste. heat the reserved ghee with the remaining 2 tbsp, add the bay leaves, black and green cardamom, cloves and cinnamon and let them crackle 40 seconds. lift the mutton out of the marinade and brown it in batches over high heat, 4 minutes a batch. return all of it to the pan. lower the flame, pour in the leftover yogurt marinade a ladle at a time and stir without stopping for 8 minutes until the fat rims the pan. add the coriander powder, kashmiri chilli, mace and salt and bhuno for 5 minutes, splashing in a little hot water each time it catches. stir in the nut paste and cook 4 minutes until it darkens a shade and smells toasted. add 500ml hot water, bring to a bare simmer, cover tightly and cook 60–70 minutes until the meat pulls off the bone. uncover and reduce 5 minutes if the gravy is looser than a pouring cream. finish with saffron milk, kewra water, grated nutmeg and the reserved birista. rest covered 10 minutes.

entries.title: Nargisi Kofta
entries.snippet: boiled eggs sheathed in spiced mutton mince, fried and halved into a korma gravy
entries.text: nargisi kofta awadhi/lucknowi boiled eggs sheathed in spiced mutton mince, fried and halved into a korma gravy gluten-free eggs mutton / lamb chana dal besan (gram flour) onion ginger garlic green chilli coriander leaves (cilantro) yogurt / dahi cashews ghee neutral oil coriander powder kashmiri chilli powder garam masala green cardamom cinnamon cloves mace (javitri) saffron water salt simmer the mince with the drained chana dal, one sliced onion, ginger and garlic pastes, salt and 150ml water until dry, about 20 minutes. cool, then grind to a stiff paste and knead in the roasted besan, green chilli, chopped coriander and half the garam masala. refrigerate 45 minutes. divide into 6, flatten each into a disc on your wet palm and wrap it around an egg, sealing every seam. deep fry two at a time in medium-hot oil, turning, until an even deep brown, 3–4 minutes. drain and set aside. for the gravy, fry the two remaining sliced onions in 2 tbsp ghee until deep brown, 12 minutes. drain, cool and grind with the soaked cashews and 4 tbsp water. heat the remaining ghee with the cardamom, cinnamon and cloves for 30 seconds, then add the onion-cashew paste and cook 5 minutes. off the heat, whisk in the yogurt in three additions, return to a low flame and stir 6 minutes until the fat separates. add the coriander powder, kashmiri chilli, mace, remaining garam masala and salt and cook 3 minutes, then pour in 350ml warm water and simmer 12 minutes. halve each kofta lengthways with a sharp knife so the egg shows, and lay them cut side up in the gravy. spoon the gravy over, add the saffron milk, cover and rest off the heat 5 minutes before serving.

entries.title: Nihari
entries.snippet: Overnight shank stew, thickened with wheat flour and finished with ginger and lime
entries.text: nihari awadhi/lucknowi overnight shank stew, thickened with wheat flour and finished with ginger and lime nut-free mutton / lamb atta (wholewheat flour) onion ginger garlic fennel powder dry ginger powder (saunth) red chilli powder turmeric powder garam masala black cardamom cinnamon bay leaf lemon / lime coriander leaves (cilantro) green chilli ghee salt brown the sliced onion in ghee, then add the ginger and garlic pastes and cook until the raw smell goes. add the powdered spices with a splash of water so they do not scorch, then the mutton. turn it in the masala over high heat until sealed. add 2 litres of water and the whole spices. bring to a boil, then drop to the barest simmer, cover, and cook 4-5 hours until the meat slides off the bone. whisk the atta into a cup of cold water until perfectly smooth and stir it into the pot. simmer 30 minutes more, stirring often, until the gravy coats a spoon. rest off the heat 20 minutes; the fat will rise. do not skim it — that layer is the point. serve with julienned ginger, green chilli, coriander and a hard squeeze of lemon at the table.

entries.title: Shahi Tukda
entries.snippet: ghee-fried bread soaked in saffron syrup under a blanket of thick rabri
entries.text: shahi tukda awadhi/lucknowi ghee-fried bread soaked in saffron syrup under a blanket of thick rabri vegetarian no-onion-garlic sliced bread ghee milk khoya / mawa sugar water saffron green cardamom pistachios almonds rose water simmer the milk in a wide heavy pan over medium-low heat, scraping the cream back in from the sides every few minutes, until reduced to about a third, 40–45 minutes. stir in the grated khoya, 3 tbsp sugar, half the saffron milk and half the cardamom powder and cook 5 minutes more. set the rabri aside to cool a little. meanwhile boil the 150g sugar with 150ml water for 5 minutes to a thin one-string syrup, then stir in the remaining saffron milk and the rose water. cut each bread slice into two triangles. fry them in ghee over medium heat until deep golden and crisp on both sides, 2 minutes a side, adding ghee as needed. drain on paper. dip each fried triangle into the warm syrup for 5 seconds a side and lift it straight out onto a serving plate. arrange the soaked bread in a single overlapping layer and spoon the warm rabri over the top. scatter with pistachios, almonds and the remaining cardamom powder. chill 1 hour before serving so the rabri sets and the bread softens through.

entries.title: Shami Kebab
entries.snippet: dense little mutton and chana dal patties, smooth inside and crisp at the edge
entries.text: shami kebab awadhi/lucknowi dense little mutton and chana dal patties, smooth inside and crisp at the edge gluten-free nut-free mutton / lamb chana dal onion garlic ginger dried red chillies black cardamom green cardamom cinnamon cloves black pepper water eggs green chilli coriander leaves (cilantro) mint garam masala lemon / lime ghee salt pressure cook the mutton, drained dal, quartered onion, garlic, ginger, whole chillies, black cardamom, green cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, peppercorns, salt and 250ml water for 5 whistles, about 20 minutes. open the lid and boil hard, stirring, until every trace of liquid has gone and the mix looks dry and sandy, 8–10 minutes. cool completely, then pick out the cinnamon stick and black cardamom shell and grind the rest to a smooth, tight paste with no added water. knead in the finely chopped onion, green chilli, coriander, mint, garam masala and the beaten egg. taste for salt now. divide into 12 and shape into flat discs 5cm across and 1.5cm thick. refrigerate 30 minutes. heat 2 tbsp ghee on a tawa over medium heat and lay in the kebabs without crowding. fry 3–4 minutes a side until a deep brown crust forms, adding the remaining ghee as you turn. drain on paper, rest 2 minutes and serve hot with lemon wedges and sliced onion.

entries.title: Sheermal
entries.snippet: slightly sweet saffron-milk flatbread, soft as brioche, brushed with ghee
entries.text: sheermal awadhi/lucknowi slightly sweet saffron-milk flatbread, soft as brioche, brushed with ghee vegetarian nut-free no-onion-garlic plain flour (maida) milk ghee sugar yogurt / dahi baking soda saffron green cardamom salt dissolve the sugar and salt in the warm milk and stir in the yogurt. mix the maida with the baking soda, rub in 60g of the melted ghee until it looks like breadcrumbs, then add half the saffron milk. add the milk mixture gradually and knead 10 minutes to a soft, smooth, slightly sticky dough. cover with a damp cloth and rest 1 hour at room temperature. knock back, divide into 8 and roll each into a disc 15cm across and 5mm thick. prick all over with a fork. bake at 220c on a preheated tray for 6–7 minutes, until the surface is set and just speckled. pull the tray out, brush each bread generously with the remaining saffron milk and melted ghee, and return for 3 minutes. dust with cardamom powder, stack under a cloth and serve warm with korma or kebabs.

entries.title: Ulte Tawe Ka Paratha
entries.snippet: wafer-thin layered paratha cooked on the back of an upturned tawa
entries.text: ulte tawe ka paratha awadhi/lucknowi wafer-thin layered paratha cooked on the back of an upturned tawa vegetarian nut-free no-onion-garlic plain flour (maida) atta (wholewheat flour) milk water ghee sugar salt mix the maida, atta, salt and sugar, rub in 2 tbsp of the melted ghee, then bring together with the warm milk and enough warm water to make a soft dough. knead 10 minutes until smooth and elastic, then cover with a damp cloth and rest 45 minutes. divide into 8 and roll one ball into a 20cm disc. brush it all over with melted ghee, dust lightly with dry maida, then cut a slit from centre to edge and roll it tightly into a cone. press the cone down onto its point into a flat pastry and rest 10 minutes. repeat with the rest. roll each pastry out to a very thin disc, 22–24cm across, working from the centre outwards. set the tawa upside down over medium heat and let it get properly hot, 4 minutes. drape a paratha over the convex surface and cook 60–90 seconds until the underside is spotted brown and it lifts freely. flip with tongs, brush with ghee and cook 60 seconds more, pressing the edges down onto the metal. crush the hot paratha lightly between your palms to open the layers and serve at once with galouti or korma.

entries.title: Zarda
entries.snippet: saffron sweet rice studded with nuts and raisins, served at the end of a dastarkhwan
entries.text: zarda awadhi/lucknowi saffron sweet rice studded with nuts and raisins, served at the end of a dastarkhwan vegetarian gluten-free no-onion-garlic basmati rice sugar ghee saffron green cardamom cloves cinnamon khoya / mawa almonds pistachios cashews raisins (kishmish) dried coconut (copra) kewra water water salt fry the almonds, pistachios, cashews and coconut in 2 tbsp ghee until just gold, 2 minutes, then the raisins for 20 seconds until they puff. drain and set aside. boil 1.2 litres of water with the salt, half the saffron milk, the cardamom and cloves. add the drained rice and cook uncovered for 6–7 minutes, until the grains are 80 percent done and still firm at the core. drain thoroughly in a colander and leave 5 minutes to steam dry. in a heavy pan melt the remaining 3 tbsp ghee, add the sugar and 100ml water and stir until it dissolves into a thin syrup, 3 minutes. fold the drained rice gently into the syrup with the remaining saffron milk, using a flat spoon and lifting rather than stirring. cover tightly, put a heavy lid or a weight on top and cook on the lowest possible heat for 15 minutes. uncover: the syrup should be absorbed and the grains separate and glossy. if wet, cook uncovered 3 minutes more. scatter over the fried nuts, raisins, crumbled khoya and kewra water, cover again and rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving warm.

entries.title: Aloo Posto
entries.snippet: potatoes cooked down in a nutty poppy seed paste, mild and quietly rich
